Wife Goes to HS Reunion, Finds Rare 1979 Dodge Magnum GT Survivor for Husband's Magnum Collection
43 photos
Photo: YouTube/Lou Costabile
What’s the grandest Mopar you can think of? It’s not a trick question – literally the most grandeur-inspiring of them all. Fine, let’s just settle for classics – which one is it? Don’t go thinking about Crown Imperials, or Chrysler 300s, or some other Plymouth VIP or Dodge Royal Lancer. It’s actually a Dodge Magnum, because the name says it is. And this guy has one of each model year, with the 1979 GT example being the crown jewel.
In everyday parlance, the word "Magnum"—derived from the Latin term for "great" or "large"—instantly conjures images of excess, potency, and larger-than-life proportions. Consumers most commonly encounter the label on oversized 1.5-liter champagne and wine bottles, indulgent ice cream bars, and king-sized beverages or snacks.
In the realm of ballistics, the designation defines large-caliber firearms and ammunition cartridges, such as the .357 Magnum and .44 Magnum, engineered to pack a far heavier propellant charge than standard rounds.
When Dodge needed a commanding moniker for its new 1978 personal luxury coupe, executives borrowed that high-caliber title to project authority during an era when federal emissions standards were strangling Detroit horsepower. Just as importantly, Dodge needed a sloped, aerodynamic nosecone to keep Richard Petty competitive on NASCAR superspeedways after the 1974 Charger expired.
Photo: YouTube/Lou Costabile The Magnum supplemented and replaced the B-body Charger SE, holding the line for two seasons before the downsized J-body Dodge Mirada replaced it in 1980.
Across the North American market, the Dodge Magnum nameplate spanned 2 distinct generations, alongside regional V8 and turbocharged 4-cylinder namesakes marketed in Brazil from 1979 to 1981 and in Mexico from 1981 to 1988. The first domestic generation ran for the 1978 and 1979 model years as the final automobile built on Chrysler's venerable rear-wheel-drive B-body mid-size platform.
Riding on a 114.9-inch wheelbase, it competed in the personal luxury segment as a two-door pillared coupe offered in XE and GT trims.
First-generation buyers paid base factory prices between $5,448 and $6,039, choosing between 318-cubic-inch, 360-CID, and 1978-only 400-cube V8 engines, all paired exclusively with a 3-speed TorqueFlite automatic transmission.
Photo: YouTube/Lou Costabile Revived after 25 years for a second domestic generation from 2005 through 2008 on the rear-wheel-drive and all-wheel-drive Chrysler LX platform, the Magnum morphed into a five-door station wagon. Offered in SE, SXT, R/T, and SRT8 trims from $22,495 to over $38,000, it packed 2.7-liter and 3.5-liter V6s or 5.7-liter and 6.1-liter Hemi V8s with 4-speed and 5-speed automatics.
After assembling 47,827 units in 1978, Dodge produced 25,367 Magnums for the 1979 model year, bringing the two-year B-body production run to 73,194 cars. Every 1979 model rolled off the Windsor, Ontario, Canada assembly line as a two-door hardtop coupe equipped with the 3-speed TorqueFlite automatic transmission, including 3,704 examples ordered with factory T-top roof panels.
Broken down by trim version, 23,693 cars were standard Magnum XEs, whereas just 1,674 buyers stepped up to the Code A75 Gran Touring (GT) package.
With the 400 big-block V8 dropped for 1979, the standard 135-hp 318 two-barrel V8 powered roughly 17,200 cars, while the optional 360 V8 came in 150-hp two-barrel tune on approximately 5,900 coupes and 195-hp four-barrel Heavy Duty Police specification on 2,226 units, including 583 GTs.
Photo: YouTube/Lou Costabile When new, a well-optioned 1979 Magnum GT 360 carried a sticker price around $8,300, squaring off directly against the Chevrolet Monte Carlo, Pontiac Grand Prix, Ford Thunderbird, Mercury Cougar XR-7, Oldsmobile Cutlass Calais, Buick Regal, and Chrysler Cordoba.
Spotting an untouched example of Chrysler's last B-body is a rare treat today, which is why automotive vlogger Lou Costabile documented Dale Lewis and his unrestored 1979 Dodge Magnum GT at the Chrysler Nationals in Carlisle, Pennsylvania. Dale got the vintage coupe in 2025, after his wife, Karen, tracked it down to complete his six-car Magnum collection, which already included a 1978 Magnum survivor and four second-generation Magnums.
Karen became the hero of the story after attending a high school committee meeting to organize a class reunion, where she reconnected with a former classmate and fellow car enthusiast who happened to own this preserved coupe . Originally delivered new through Trail Dodge in Inver Grove Heights, Minnesota, the car still wears its red dealer emblem on the left side of the trunk lid and displays just 48,599 original miles in the center of its 85-mph speedometer (more to the point, it did so in July, 2026).
Photo: YouTube/Lou Costabile The fender tag decodes the E57 360 V8 (two-barrel), a D36 for the A727 3-speed TorqueFlite transmission, A75 Magnum GT package, DLR4 deluxe red leather low-back bucket seats (Code C55), C16 center console, H51 air conditioning, B41 power front disc brakes, G11 tinted glass, G52 left remote mirror, and J25 3-speed intermittent wipers.
Outside, the Spinnaker White body features color-keyed GT wheel flares, 15x7-inch GT road wheels, retractable clear headlight covers, and worn original pinstripes that Dale refuses to replace. Swinging open the long doors reveals a plush crimson interior where XE badges still sit in the woodgrain door trim, paired with the GT-exclusive engine-turned aluminum dash and console appliques that recall a Pontiac Trans Am.
Between the red leather bucket seats rests the console-mounted shifter, facing a full instrument cluster with oil pressure and alternator gauges, a rear defogger switch, and the original AM/FM stereo radio, while the trunk holds a space-saver spare and a 1979 sales brochure.
Photo: YouTube/Lou Costabile Underhood, a time-capsule 1979 engine bay houses the 360 V8, rated at 150 hp and 265 lb-ft of torque. Remarkably, the air cleaner still retains its factory Electronic Spark Control System computer—a Lean Burn module most owners tore off on day two—alongside the first-year diagnostic plug, battery heat shield washer reservoir, and assembly line inspection chalk marks.
Even among the better part of 3,000 Mopars gathered at Carlisle this past summer, Dale counts only no more than seven Magnums on the show field. Never mind highways – he’s never seen another on the road. Once Karen retires, the couple plans to take this comfortable 1979 survivor on a Route 66 road trip.
